Subject: Complete Denture
Question: In making a final impression for a complete denture, the most important area of the impression is
Option A: Ridge area of maxilla and buccal shelf of mandible
Option C: Junction of hard and soft palate of maxilla and disto lingual area of mandible
Option D: Mid palatal area of maxilla and ridge of the mandible
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 10th ed 182,211 / Winkler 2nd ed 89,90]

The junction of hard and soft palate of maxilla and the disto lingual area of mandible are the most important areas since proper extension and seal in these regions is critical for retention and stability of the complete denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The stability of a mandibular complete denture will be enhanced when
Option A: The level of occlusal plane is above the dorsum of the tongue
Option B: The tongue rests on the occlusal surface
Option C: The lingual contour of the denture is concave
Option D: The posterior teeth on the denture have a broad buccolingual width
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 10th ed 176 / Winkler 2nd ed 50]

The dentures should be shaped and polished such that the tongue and cheek tends to seat rather than unseat the dentures. If the posterior teeth are too wide buccolingually the tongue and cheeks will unseat the dentures. When the tongue rests on the occlusal surface, it helps seat the mandibular denture, enhancing stability.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The primary, stress bearing area of maxillary complete denture is
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 10th ed 151]

The compact bone in combination with tightly attached dense submucosa and keratinised mucosa makes the alveolar ridge area resistant to occlusal forces. Hence the alveolar ridge is the primary stress bearing area in the maxillary complete denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The mean denture bearing area in the edentulous mandible is approximately
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 232]

According to the 12th edition, the average available denture base area for an edentulous mandible is 14 cm² and for maxilla is 24 cm².

Note: According to 10th edition the mean denture bearing area of edentulous mandible was reported as 12.25 cm².

Embedded question: The mean denture bearing area of the mandible and maxilla respectively is (MED-14)
a) 12.25 cm² and 24 cm²
b) 14 cm² and 24 cm² ← Correct (12th edition)
c) 14 mm² and 24 mm²
d) 24 cm² and 14 cm²

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: While taking impression of flabby fibrous tissue on maxillary ridge for complete denture care is taken to:
Option B: Not maintain intimate contact with tissues
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 10th ed 174, 224]

The flabby tissue will interfere with stability of denture. The best treatment is finger massage or surgical removal to improve the denture foundation area. While taking impression of flabby fibrous tissue, a tray with a spacer (window tray or sectional tray) is used so that the flabby tissue is not displaced and recorded in its resting position using mucostatic technique.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: In primary impression the stock tray should be ___ mm larger than ridge.
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 221 / Winkler 2nd ed 91]

If the tray is too large, it will distort the tissues around the borders of impression. If it is too small, the border tissues will collapse inward onto the residual ridge and thus reduce the support for the dentures. The stock tray should be approximately 6 mm larger than the ridge to allow adequate thickness of impression material.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Passive impression technique involves:
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 10th ed 224]

Passive impression technique is also known as mucostatic or pressure-less impression technique. It records the tissues with minimal distortion and causes the least possible displacement of tissues. There will be large amount of space between the tray and soft tissues. It uses a very fluid type of impression material. Impression plaster is the common material used in this technique.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Primary stress bearing area in mandibular edentulous ridge is:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 238]

The buccal shelf area is covered with cortical bone which is usually at right angles to occlusal forces. For this reason, it offers excellent resistance to occlusal forces and takes off the occlusal load imposed on the sharp narrow crest of the alveolar ridge. Hence the buccal shelf is the primary stress bearing area in the mandibular edentulous ridge.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Alginate at 20 degrees, the gel is formed in
Explanation:
'A' [Gurukeerat Singh 2nd ed 348]

The gelation temperature of alginate is in the range of 18–20 degrees Celsius. The fibrils of the gel are formed chemically by primary bonds.

The working time of alginate:
• Type 1 (fast set): 1.5–2 min
• Type 2 (slow set): 3–4 min

At 20 degrees, the gel formation (setting) occurs in approximately 3–4 minutes.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Retromolar pad:
Option A: Should not be covered by lower denture
Option B: Should be covered by lower denture
Option C: Has tendon of temporalis muscle attached to it
Option D: Disappears on eruption of mandibular last molars
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 239]

Retromolar pad:
• The retromolar pad must be covered by denture to perfect the border seal in this region.
• Gives distal extension limit.
• Gives height of occlusal plane.
• This area contains glandular tissue and fibres of temporalis tendon, buccinator, superior pharyngeal constrictor and pterygomandibular raphae.
• All these limiting structures prevent placement of extra pressure on retromolar pad during impression procedures.
• The denture base should extend up to approximately one half to two thirds over the retromolar pad.
• Though retromolar pad provides stability, support and retention, the main objective of covering it is retention.

Retromolar pad does not have insertion of (AIPG-2015):
a) Fibers of buccinators  b) Medial pterygoid  c) Pterygomandibular raphe  d) Temporalis

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Which material is carried in a custom tray?
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 10th ed 240]

Silicone or metallic oxide paste or rubber base materials are used in a custom tray during final impression. These materials are accurate, dimensionally stable, and flow well in custom trays.

Impression compound, reversible hydrocolloid (Agar-Agar), and irreversible hydrocolloid (alginate) are used in a stock tray for preliminary impression.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The following property of saliva affects denture retention:
Option A: Quality & Quantity of serous & mucus saliva
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 438]

The quality and quantity of both serous and mucous saliva affect denture retention. Saliva acts as the adhesive medium between the denture base and oral tissues. Thin, watery serous saliva provides better adhesion, while thick, viscous (mucous) saliva reduces retention. Both types and their quantities thus affect the overall retention of the denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: How should the lingual extension of the mandibular impression be tested?
Option A: By functional movements of the facial muscles
Option B: By vigorous extreme movements of the tongue
Option C: By functional movements of the tongue
Option D: By lateral and protrusive movement of the mandible
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 246, 247]

The lingual extension of the mandibular impression should be tested by functional movements of the tongue (option C). The tongue should perform normal, functional movements (not extreme or vigorous) such as touching the roof of the mouth, lips and cheeks to check if the lingual flange extension is correct.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The relationship of the denture base that resists dislodgement of denture in horizontal direction is:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 10th ed 171]

Stability is the resistance of the denture to horizontal movements or lateral forces. It resists dislodgement of the denture in the horizontal direction.

• Retention: resistance to removal from tissue surface (vertical)
• Support: resistance to occlusal forces (vertical toward ridge)
• Stability: resistance to horizontal/lateral shifting

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Denture bearing area of the ridge is
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 214]

The denture bearing area (stress-bearing area) of the ridge is covered by keratinised mucosa. Keratinised mucosa is firmer and more resistant to the forces of mastication, making it suitable for bearing the occlusal loads transferred through the denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The thickness of the spacer used in special tray is
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 225]

Wax spacer, approximately 1 mm thickness, is used to provide the space in the tray for the final impression material and allows the tray to be properly positioned in the mouth during border-moulding procedures. Baseplate wax covers the basal seat area except for labial and buccal reflections and the posterior palatal seal area.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The main purpose of covering the retromolar pad area is
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 239 / Winkler 2nd ed 90]

The main purpose of covering the retromolar pad area is retention. The retromolar pad must be covered by denture to perfect the border seal in this region. Although retromolar pad provides stability, support and retention, the main objective of covering it is RETENTION through border seal.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Selective pressure impression technique indicated in
Option A: Firm healthy mucosal covering over the ridge
Option D: When sharp bony spicules are present in the ridge
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 10th ed 224]

Selective pressure impression technique is indicated in firm, healthy mucosal covering over the ridge (option A). This technique distributes load to acceptable areas.

For options B, C, D (flabby ridges, knife edge with movable mucosa, sharp bony spicules), mucostatic impression technique is used since these conditions require minimal displacement of tissues.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Emergency retentive force is:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 441]

Atmospheric pressure is called the emergency retentive force or temporary restraining force. The weight of atmospheric pressure is about 14.7 lb/in². It is effective only where there is adequate peripheral seal. When the peripheral seal is broken temporarily, atmospheric pressure becomes the emergency force that maintains the denture in position.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: An important factor that aids in stability of complete denture is
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 414]

Balanced occlusion (harmonious occlusion) in which the teeth are placed in neutral zone without any premature contacts helps in stability of denture.

Balanced occlusion in complete denture is essential for: (APPG-2016)
a) Esthetics  b) Support  c) Stability  d) Retention
Answer: Stability

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: To make an impression of hyperplastic tissue one should
Option B: Use elastomeric impressions to displace the tissues
Option C: Ensure intimate contact of impression material to the tissue
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 10th ed 174, 224]

The impression of hyperplastic tissue is recorded in passive state using mucostatic or pressure-less technique. The goal is to ensure the impression material comes into intimate contact with the tissue WITHOUT displacing it. This passive contact ensures that the denture will fit properly in the tissue's resting position, providing optimal retention.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The zinc-oxide eugenol impression paste is used to enhance quality of:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 10th ed 175]

Advantages of ZOE (zinc oxide eugenol) paste when used to enhance quality of modeling compound impression:
a) Accurate borders are formed, since the material is more plastic in nature.
b) Does not absorb the mucous secretions produced in palate and thus accurately records the palatal part of impression.
c) Does not require a separating medium.

ZOE paste is applied over the set compound impression to record fine details of the oral mucosa (wash impression technique).

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Muscle which has influence in the formation of buccal frenum of maxilla
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 239]

Buccal frenum of maxilla contains Caninus (Levator anguli oris) muscle fibers.

Buccal frenum of mandible contains Triangularis (depressor anguli oris) muscle fibers.

There are 3 freni (1 labial + 2 buccal) in maxilla and 4 freni (1 labial + 2 buccal + 1 lingual) in mandible.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Atmospheric pressure as a factor of retention is effective only
Option B: If adequate peripheral seal is present
Option C: If principle of mucostatics is applied
Option D: If good neuromuscular co-ordination is present
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 441]

Atmospheric pressure as a factor of retention is effective only if adequate peripheral seal is present. The peripheral seal creates a seal at the borders of the denture that prevents air from entering beneath the denture base. This allows atmospheric pressure (14.7 lb/in²) to exert force on the outer surface of the denture to maintain it in position.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The purpose of boxing an impression is
Option A: Boxing preserves the border width after border molding
Option B: To serve as a base for cast poured
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 229]

The purpose of boxing an impression is:
a) To preserve the border width and contour after border molding
b) To serve as a base for the cast to be poured
Both A and B are correct, hence the answer is C.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: If a complete denture patient has genial tubercle at the level of the crest of mandibular ridge, the denture base:
Option C: Should cover them but relief is not necessary
Option D: Should cover them and relief is must
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 107, 234]

If a complete denture patient has genial tubercle at the level of the crest of mandibular ridge, the denture base should cover them and relief is a must. The genial tubercles (mental spines) are bony projections on the inner surface of the mandible. When they are at the crest level due to bone resorption, they must be covered by the denture but with adequate relief to avoid pressure necrosis and discomfort.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The masseteric notch in distobuccal corners of the mandibular denture is due to
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 239 / Winkler 2nd ed 90]

The masseteric notch (or anti-masseteric notch) in distobuccal corners of the mandibular denture is due to the action of masseter on buccinator. During jaw movements, the masseter muscle displaces the buccinator, creating a notch at the distobuccal border of the mandibular denture. The flange must be shaped to accommodate this action.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Lower denture in anterior region is limited by the following (except):
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 239, 243]

Lower denture in anterior region is limited by (except Modiolus):
• Origin of genioglossus (option C) limits lower denture in anterior region.
• Sublingual salivary glands (option D) limit lower denture in anterior region.
• Mylohyoid muscle (option B) limits the denture in molar region.
• Modiolus (option A) is a fibromuscular condensation at the corner of the mouth; it does not directly limit the anterior lower denture extension.

Note: The distal most part of the lingual surface of the denture is influenced by palatoglossus and superior constrictor muscle.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The lingual surface in molar region in mandibular denture is determined by
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 239]

The mylohyoid muscle determines the lingual surface in the molar region of the mandibular denture. The mylohyoid ridge and muscle form the lingual border at the molar region. During impression making, the mylohyoid muscle must be displaced in functional movements to record the lingual extension in the molar region accurately.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Custom tray is better than stock tray for impression of complete denture due to following reasons, except:
Option A: Custom tray is easy to adapt
Option B: Stock tray may not record full flange
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 10th ed 175]

Custom tray is NOT cheaper than stock tray — this is the incorrect (exception) statement. Custom trays are more expensive to fabricate as they require additional clinical and laboratory steps.

All other statements are true advantages of custom tray over stock tray:
• Custom tray is easy to adapt to the ridge form
• Stock tray may not record full flange properly
• Stock tray can distort easily due to its flexibility

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Oral tissues are best recorded in functional state by
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 478]

Mucocompressive impression technique records the oral tissues in their functional (compressed) state. In this technique, the tissues are compressed during impression making, similar to the functional state during mastication. The resulting denture fits the tissues when they are under functional load.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Denture stability refers to resistance of a denture:
Option A: To move in a vertical direction away from basal seat
Option B: To move in a vertical dimension towards basal seat
Option C: To movements on its tissue foundation especially to lateral forces
Option D: Against any kind of movement more than 24 μm in any direction
Explanation:
'C' [Nallaswamy 1st ed 64]

Objectives of impression:
• Retention: It is the resistance to displacement away from tissue surface. It is a mucosa-borne phenomenon.
• Support: It is the resistance to the occlusal forces in the vertical direction. It is a bone-borne phenomenon.
• Stability: It is resistance to lateral shifting and movements on tissue foundation.
• Preservation of remaining structures.

Denture stability refers to resistance to movements on its tissue foundation, especially to lateral forces (option C).

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Functional impression technique can be applied in
Explanation:
'A' [McCrackens 13th ed 241]

Functional impression technique can be applied only in uniformly firm ridge consistency (option A). This technique records the tissues in their functional state under load. It is contraindicated for:
• Knife-edge ridges (option C) — too painful under load
• Displaceable/flabby ridges (option D) — tissue displacement occurs
• Not suitable for all variety of ridges

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Masseter muscle is a powerful muscle because of
Option D: Its attachment to bone is unique
Explanation:
'B' [Sichers Oral Anatomy 153]

Masseter muscle is a powerful muscle because of its multipennate arrangement of fibres (option B). Multipennate muscles have fibres attached to a central tendon from multiple sides, allowing more force generation per unit area than parallel, unipennate, or bipennate arrangements. This arrangement maximizes the physiological cross-sectional area of the muscle.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: In making complete denture for maxilla?
Option A: Relief is given for incisive foramen in all cases
Option B: Relief is provided when there is compression of Nasopalatine vessels
Option D: Relief given when foramen approaches crest of bone
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed (Incisive papilla section)]

The incisive papilla is a small tissue projection located immediately behind and between the central incisors. It covers the incisive foramen through which the nasopalatine nerves and vessels pass.

• Relief is provided when there is compression of nasopalatine vessels (option B).
• If relief is not provided, it can cause paraesthesia, pain, burning sensation and other vague complaints.
• Relief is provided specifically when compression of the nasopalatine vessels and nerves is anticipated or when the foramen is on the crest of the resorbed ridge.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Which muscle has an indirect effect on the extent of impression in labial vestibule (maxilla)
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 11th ed 147]

The fibers of orbicularis oris pass horizontally through the lips and anastomose with the fibers of the buccinator muscle. Because the fibers run in a horizontal direction, it has only an indirect effect on the extent of an impression in the labial vestibule and hence on the denture flange. This indirect action through horizontal fiber arrangement makes orbicularis oris the answer.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Esthetics starts with:
Explanation:
'A' [Heartwell 5th ed 227]

In an impression technique for complete dentures, the procedures must strive for five primary objectives:
• Support
• Stability
• Esthetics
• Retention
• Preservation of remaining residual ridge

Esthetics is one of the five primary objectives and it starts right from the very first procedure — taking impression — since the impression determines the foundation upon which all esthetic elements are built.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Which one of the following is not essential for primary impression:
Explanation:
'C' [Heartwell 5th ed 227]

The primary objectives of complete denture impression are:
• Retention
• Stability
• Esthetics
• Support
• Preservation of remaining residual structures

Phonetics (option C) is NOT listed as one of the primary essential objectives of taking a primary impression. While phonetics is an important aspect of complete denture therapy overall, it is not an essential requirement specifically for the impression procedures.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Disinfection duration of alginate impressions when immersion method is used should not exceed
Explanation:
'A' [Phillips 11th ed 246]

The current protocol for disinfecting hydrocolloid (alginate) impressions is to use household bleach (1:10 dilution), iodophors or synthetic phenols. The time of immersion should not exceed 10 minutes when immersion method is used. Prolonged immersion causes dimensional changes in the alginate impression.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: A ten-year-old complete denture wearer wants replacement of his denture. The most suitable impression technique in this case is
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 239]

Selective pressure technique is the most widely respected and accepted theory by transferring load to acceptable areas. For a 10-year-old complete denture wearer requiring replacement, the ridges would have undergone considerable resorption and the tissues are adaptive. Selective pressure technique is appropriate as it distributes load selectively to stress-bearing areas.

Minimal pressure technique is a compromise between mucostatic and mucocompressive techniques, but the amount of pressure to be applied cannot be assessed and ensured, so it is not used eventually.

Pressure technique has its disadvantage by placing tissue under continuous pressure.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Emergency retentive force for the maxillary complete denture is
Explanation:
'D' [Nallaswamy 1st ed Pg 63]

The base of the tongue may also serve as an emergency retentive force for some patients. It rises up at the back and presses against the distal border of the maxillary denture in the retromolar areas. This is done without conscious effort when the patient bites into an apple or sandwich. It is seldom that a patient needs to be taught how to do this.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: In the treatment plan of a conventional immediate complete dentures, the anterior teeth are extracted:
Explanation:
'D' [Nallaswamy 1st ed 258]

In the treatment plan of a conventional immediate complete denture:
• Anterior teeth on the master cast are broken away, trimmed upto the cervical margin and smoothened.
• The ridge lap (cervical) portion of the artificial teeth are trimmed and arranged on the master cast.
• Artificial teeth are arranged over the area where the natural teeth were present; the arrangement should be in harmony with existing teeth as well as the prosthetic teeth.
• The denture is flasked, dewaxed, packed, processed, and finished.
• During the insertion appointment, the remaining anterior teeth are extracted as atraumatically as possible, preserving the soft tissues and bone. The finished denture is seated in patient's mouth.

So anterior teeth are extracted AFTER making the immediate denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The retromolar pads as a landmark is
Explanation:
'B' [Zarb & Bolender 12th ed 239]

The retromolar pads as a landmark is relatively stable. Unlike many anatomical landmarks that change with ridge resorption, the retromolar pad remains relatively stable in position. This stability makes it a reliable landmark for determining the height of the occlusal plane and the posterior extension of the mandibular denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The purpose of relieving mid-palatine area in complete dentures is to prevent
Explanation:
'B' [Bouchers 11th ed 142 / Nallaswamy 1st ed 54]

Mid palatine raphe is the median suture area covered by a thin submucosa and the mucosa layer is practically in contact with the underlying bone. For this reason, the soft tissue covering the median palatal suture is non-resilient and may need to be relieved to avoid trauma from the denture base. Relief in this area prevents midline fractures in the denture caused by the bony median palatal raphe acting as a fulcrum.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The mandibular labial frenum is a fibrous band that can be influenced by
Explanation:
'D' [Nallaswamy 1st ed 55 / Winkler 2nd ed 90]

The mandibular labial frenum is a fibrous band that can be influenced by the incisivus and orbicularis oris muscles. Unlike the maxillary labial frenum, the mandibular labial frenum is active because of its attachments from the orbicularis oris.

Embedded question (AIIMS NOV-14): Thick muscular labial frenum is because of?
a) Septal muscle  b) Orbicularis oris  c) Buccinator  d) Nasopalatine muscle
Answer: b) Orbicularis oris

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Setting time of plaster is influenced by
Explanation:
'D' [Phillips 11th ed 264–265]

Setting time of plaster of Paris is influenced by all of the following:
• W/P ratio: If W/P ratio increases, setting time increases (more water → slower set).
• Speed of mixing: The longer and more rapidly the plaster is mixed, the shorter is the setting time.
• Adding gypsum (<20%): Acts as an accelerator — gypsum crystals act as nuclei for crystallization.
• Also accelerated by: Potassium sulphate, NaCl (<25%).
• Retarded by: Borax, blood, plasma proteins.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: While taking final impression tray should be seated first:
Option C: Anteriorly or posteriorly depending upon operators choice
Explanation:
'A' [Zarb & Bolender 12th ed 229]

The tray should be seated first anteriorly with the labial notch acting as a guide for the placement of the tray in the patient's mouth for making final impression. This is most easily achieved by observing the position of the labial frenum relative to the labial notch in the tray. When the frenum is positioned within the notch, the index fingers are shifted to the molar region to apply pressure.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: While making impression of flabby fibrous tissues on maxillary ridge for complete denture Prosthesis, care is taken to
Option B: Use selective pressure technique of impression making
Explanation:
'A' [Winkler 2nd ed 62 / Rangarajan 1st ed 77]

Management of fibrous flabby tissue (most commonly in maxillary anterior region) is by:
• Surgical removal
• Non-surgical (mucostatic technique): if the tissue is localized and doesn't interfere with the stability of the denture.

The key aspect of the non-surgical management is the choice of impression technique:
• Use mucostatic technique to obtain maximum retention without displacing the flabby tissue.
• Mucostatic technique does not displace the flabby tissue and the denture maintains contact with the tissue in the resting position, thereby providing optimal retention.

Flabby ridge is seen most commonly in (MHCET-15): Anterior maxilla

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Which of the following are stress bearing areas?
Option A: Buccal shelf area, incisive papilla and palatine rugae
Option B: Slopes of residual ridge, palatine rugae and midpalatine raphe
Option C: Incisive papilla, slope of the residual ridge and crest of the residual ridge
Option D: Slope of residual ridge, buccal shelf area and hard palate
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's Synopsis Point No. 24]

Stress-bearing areas of complete denture:

Maxillary denture:
• Primary: Alveolar ridge (slopes)
• Secondary: Hard palate

Mandibular denture:
• Primary: Buccal shelf
• Secondary: Slopes of residual ridge, retromolar pads

Correct stress-bearing areas include: Slope of residual ridge (maxilla), buccal shelf area (mandible), and hard palate — all represented in option D.

Non-stress bearing areas: Incisive papilla, midpalatine raphe, incisive foramen area.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: The non-pressure or the mucostatic techniques of impression making was introduced by
Explanation:
'A' [Rangarajan 1st ed 41]

Harry L. Page introduced the mucostatic (non-pressure/pressure-less) impression technique in 1938. In this technique, the tissues are recorded in their resting state with minimal or no pressure applied.

Other attributions:
• Selective pressure = Boucher
• Hall automatic articulator = Hall

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the elastomeric impression taken in a custom tray?
Option B: Custom tray is the best method of choice of impression taking
Option C: Impression is not distorted in custom tray
Option D: If compressed lightly then it is easier to remove
Explanation:
'D' [Schillinberg 3rd ed 290]

Clinical advantages obtained with the use of custom trays over stock trays:
1. Controls size and conserves volume of material. Minimizes polymerization-induced shrinkage, reduces patient discomfort and cost.
2. Provides dimensional accuracy and stability with uniform thickness of material throughout.
3. Custom tray rigidity reduces potential for distortion in comparison to flexible stock trays.
4. Use of tray adhesive is not required.

Option D is INCORRECT: If the elastomeric impression is compressed lightly, it is NOT easier to remove — it actually distorts the impression due to elastic recovery creating dimensional inaccuracies. This makes option D the incorrect statement.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Torquing movement in maxillary denture is avoided by?
Explanation:
'D' [Schillinberg 3rd ed 290]

Lateral torquing forces and horizontal forces are best resisted by adequate border seal (stability) in maxillary denture. Torquing movements are avoided by border seal which prevents lateral displacement.

Adhesion, cohesion and interfacial surface tension help in achieving denture retention (resistance to removal in direction opposite to insertion), but do not resist torquing movements specifically.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Most common reason to repeat impression is?
Explanation:
'A' [Nallaswamy 1st ed 90]

The most common reason to repeat an impression is improper positioning of the impression tray. If the tray is tilted or shifted to one side, the flange of the impression on the side of deviation will be excessively thick while the flange on the opposite side will be thin.

Other reasons to repeat include: improper consistency, large voids, movement of the tray during setting, and too little or too much impression material.

Subject: Complete Denture
Question: Dull appearance of mouth temperature wax indicates
Option C: Contact of the material with tissues
Explanation:
'D' [Nallaswamy 1st ed 87]

The mouth temperature wax impression is removed after 4–6 minutes and examined:
• Glossy areas = tissue contact has occurred.
• Dull areas = areas NOT in contact with the tissues (need additional wax).

Dull appearance indicates PARTIAL contact or lack of contact (option D).

Note: With green stick compound (different from mouth temperature wax):
• Dull areas = contact
• Glossy areas = no contact

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The upper denture falls when the patient opens his mouth wide. This is due to:
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 227, 217]

The thickness of the distobuccal flange of maxilla must be adjusted to accommodate the ramus, coronoid process and the masseter. If the flange is too thick, the coronoid process will push the denture out of place during opening or lateral movements of mandible. Hence, a thick disto-buccal flange causes the upper denture to fall when the patient opens his mouth wide.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Distolingual extension of the mandibular impression for a complete denture is limited by the action of:
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 247]

The distolingual extension of the mandibular impression is limited by the superior constrictor muscle. Anteriorly the lingual flange is determined by genioglossus; by mylohyoid in molar region and by superior constrictor and palatoglossus in the posterior region.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: PPS anatomically is:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 217]

PPS (posterior palatal seal) anatomically corresponds to the pterygomaxillary notches and fovea palatine. The posterior palatal seal area extends from one pterygomaxillary (hamular) notch to the other across the posterior border of the hard palate, passing through the fovea palatinae.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Secondary peripheral seal area in mandible is provided by:
Explanation:
'B' [Winkler 2nd ed 90]

The secondary peripheral seal area in mandible is provided by the anterior lingual border. The primary peripheral seal in the mandibular denture is the entire border or periphery of the denture. The anterior lingual border provides secondary seal in the lingual sulcus region.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Increased depth in posterior palatal seal area of denture causes:
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 342, 343]

Increased depth in the posterior palatal seal area of denture causes unseating of the denture base. The width of posterior palatal seal is limited to a bead on the denture that is 1–1.5 mm high and 1.5 mm broad at its base with sharp apex. A greater depth creates an area of tissue displacement which pushes the denture downwards (unseats it).

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The posterior palatal seal for a maxillary complete denture:
Option A: Is placed immediately posterior to the vibrating line
Option B: Is placed immediately anterior to the vibrating line
Option C: Is not necessary if a metal base is made
Option D: Will vary in outline and depth according to the palatal form
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 343]

Posterior palatal seal and soft palate type:

| Soft palate type | PPS characteristics |
|---|---|
| Slight downward slope (Class I) | Widest PPS, most posterior |
| Moderate slope (Class II) | Medium |
| Near vertical (Class III / high vault) | Narrowest PPS, most anterior |

The PPS will vary in outline and depth according to the palatal form (option D). A flat palate gives widest PPS while a high-vaulted palate gives narrowest PPS.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Coronoid process:
Option A: Limits the extension of maxillary posterior teeth setting
Option B: Limits the extent of the distobuccal flange of the upper complete denture
Option C: Limits the thickness of the distobuccal flange of the denture
Option D: Limits the movement of the maxillary denture during lateral excursions
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 10th ed 157]

The coronoid process limits the extent (and thickness) of the distobuccal flange of the upper complete denture. During mandibular opening and lateral movements, the coronoid process moves anteriorly and inferiorly under the zygomatic arch. If the distobuccal flange of the maxillary denture is too thick or too extensive, the coronoid process will contact and displace the denture.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The function of posterior palatal seal is:
Option B: To aid in insertion and removal of complete denture
Option C: Will seal thus helping in retention of maxillary complete denture
Option D: Retention of mandibular denture by sealing its posterior margin
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 342]

Functions of posterior palatal seal:
• Slightly displaces the tissues at the distal end of denture to ensure a close adaptation and retention of denture.
• Prevents ingress of food and saliva beneath denture base.
• Prevents excess impression material from running down the patient's throat.
• Creates a partial vacuum beneath the maxillary denture, enhancing retention.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The buccal frenal attachment of mandibular denture should be trimmed and rounded to allow proper function of
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 238]

The buccal frenum of maxilla contains Caninus or levator anguli oris.
The buccal frenum of mandible contains Triangularis (depressor anguli oris).

The buccal frenal attachment of mandibular denture should be trimmed and rounded to allow proper function of the triangularis (depressor anguli oris) muscle.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Over extension of the posterior border of the denture causes
Option C: Sagging of the corners of the mouth
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 44, 422]

Over extension of the posterior border of the denture causes gagging sensation (option A). The overextended posterior border stimulates the gag reflex. Epulis fissuratum occurs due to overextension of the FLANGES (not the posterior border). Sagging of corners of mouth occurs due to incorrect vertical dimension or incorrect occlusal plane.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Distal palatal termination of the maxillary complete denture base is dictated by the:
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 342, 422]

The vibrating line extends from one pterygomaxillary notch to the other. The distal end of the maxillary denture should extend 1 or 2 mm posterior to the vibrating line. This ensures that the posterior palatal seal is on the movable soft palate for proper sealing.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Incorporation of peripheral seal in an impression is necessary to obtain:
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 10th ed 183, 433]

Incorporation of peripheral seal (border moulding) in an impression is necessary to obtain a functionally moulded periphery. Border moulding records the functional extensions of the denture borders, creating an accurate seal at the periphery of the denture that aids in retention.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: In determining the posterior limit of a maxillary denture base, which of the following is on the posterior border?
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 342, 422]

In determining the posterior limit of a maxillary denture base, the hamular notch (pterygomaxillary notch) is on the posterior border. The posterior palatal seal area extends from one hamular notch to the other across the posterior hard palate. The vibrating line is anterior to the hamular notch and also guides the posterior limit.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Vibrating line is on the
Option B: Junction of hard and soft palate
Option D: At the junction of muscularis uvulae and palatine muscle
Explanation:
'C' [Boucher's 12th ed 217]

The vibrating line marks the beginning of motion in the soft palate when the patient says 'ah' and it passes about 2 mm in front of fovea palatinae. The vibrating line is ALWAYS present on the soft palate (option C). It does NOT lie on the hard palate or exactly at the junction of hard and soft palate.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Post dam area serves mainly to:
Option A: Prevent ingress of food and saliva beneath denture base
Option B: Preventing lifting away of denture during incising
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 343]

Post dam area (posterior palatal seal) serves mainly to prevent lifting away of the maxillary denture during incising. During anterior incision, the denture is subjected to lifting forces at the posterior border. The post dam creates a seal that resists this lifting tendency.

Additional functions: prevents ingress of food/saliva, creates partial vacuum for retention.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Distobuccal flange of mandibular denture is influenced by
Explanation:
'A' [Boucher's 12th ed 239]

The distobuccal flange of mandibular denture is influenced by the masseter and buccinator muscles. The labial flange of mandible is determined by buccinator and masseter. The action of buccinator occurs in a horizontal direction, so it cannot lift the denture. The distobuccal borders of mandible must converge rapidly to avoid displacement by the masseter muscle.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Broad palatal seal indicates
Explanation:
'B' [Winkler 2nd ed / AP-02]

Broad palatal seal indicates Type B palatal form. The classification of palatal forms:
• Type A: High vaulted (V-shaped) palate → narrow, deep PPS
• Type B: Medium/U-shaped palate → medium or broad PPS
• Type C: Flat palate → widest PPS

Broad palatal seal is characteristic of Type B palatal form.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Which of the following is not a mouth temperature wax:
Explanation:
'C' [Winkler 2nd ed 118]

Mouth temperature waxes used to record PPS in fluid wax technique include: Adaptol, Iowa wax, and Korecta wax No. 4.

HI (HL) physiologic paste (option C) is a metallic oxide paste — NOT a wax. It is an impression paste, not a mouth temperature wax. Therefore, HL physiologic paste is NOT a mouth temperature wax.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Posterior palatal seal is recorded when the head is bent at
Explanation:
'A' [Winkler 2nd ed 118]

In the conventional method of recording PPS, the patient is seated in an upright position. In the fluid wax technique, PPS is recorded when the head is bent at 30°. During recording of PPS, the patient's head should be positioned such that the Frankfort horizontal plane is 30 degrees below the horizontal plane. At this position, the muscles of the soft palate are at maximum downwards and forward functional position. This also prevents aspiration of impression material and saliva.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Instructing the patient to say 'ah' with short vigorous bursts will help in visualizing
Option D: Junction of hard and soft palate
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 217, 226 / Winkler 2nd ed 111]

Instructing the patient to say 'ah' with short vigorous bursts will help in visualizing the posterior vibrating line. When the patient says 'ah', the soft palate moves. The boundary between the moving and non-moving portions of the palate — the posterior vibrating line — becomes visible during this movement.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Fovea palatine are situated in:
Option C: At the junction of hard and soft palate
Explanation:
'B' [Boucher's 12th ed 217, 342 / Winkler 2nd ed 108]

Fovea palatinae are indentations near the midline of the palate formed by coalescence of several mucous gland ducts. They are ALWAYS on the soft palate, located 2 mm behind the vibrating line. They serve as a landmark for the posterior palatal seal area.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Which muscle has dual function as related to Complete Denture
Explanation:
'C' [AP-94, 02]

The buccinator muscle has a dual function as related to complete dentures:
1. It determines the buccal corridor and buccal flanges of the denture.
2. Its action (horizontal direction) prevents displacement of both maxillary and mandibular dentures.

The buccinator affects both the upper and lower denture borders — making it the muscle with dual function in complete denture fabrication.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The correctly placed posterior palatal seal creates:
Option A: Vacuum in posterior part of palate
Option C: Partial vacuum beneath the maxillary denture
Option D: A close adaptation of maxillary denture at tuberosity
Explanation:
'C' [Winkler 2nd ed 107–108]

The primary purpose of PPS is the retention of the maxillary denture. PPS creates a PARTIAL vacuum beneath the maxillary denture (option C). This partial vacuum is activated only when horizontal or tipping forces are directed against the denture base. The duration of this vacuum is small and so little or no irreversible alterations to the underlying mucosa will take place.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Anterior vibrating line is located on:
Option C: Either on soft or hard palatal tissue
Explanation:
'A' [Winkler 2nd ed 110–111]

The anterior vibrating line is located on the soft palatal tissue (option A). There are two vibrating lines:
• Anterior vibrating line: Located at the junction of the non-moving hard palate and the movable soft palate — always on SOFT palatal tissue, passing through or just posterior to the fovea palatinae.
• Posterior vibrating line: Where the soft palate begins maximum movement.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Mandibular complete denture should cover retromolar pad because
Option A: More surface area gives better retention
Option D: Retromolar pad contains glandular tissue, buccinator fibers, temporalis fibers, and pterygomandibular raphe
Explanation:
'D' [Boucher's 12th ed 239 / Winkler 2nd ed 90]

Mandibular complete denture should cover retromolar pad because it contains glandular tissue, fibres of buccinator, temporalis tendon, superior pharyngeal constrictor and pterygomandibular raphae. These structures help in border seal, and the soft glandular tissue allows slight compression for retention. The main objective of covering it is retention through border seal.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Posterior palatal seal is seen in
Option C: Junction of hard and soft palate
Explanation:
'B' [Winkler 2nd ed 11]

Posterior palatal seal is seen/present on the soft palate (option B). The PPS must be placed on movable tissue (soft palate) to create a seal. A seal on hard palate (immovable) would not provide the dynamic sealing effect needed.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: A High Tracing Device is used for
Explanation:
'A' [Winkler 2nd ed 196]

A High Tracing Device (Gothic arch tracer) is used for extra-oral graphic tracings. Jaw movements can be recorded by the simple tracer assembly method. Tracing may be extraoral or intraoral.

Extraoral tracers include:
• High extraoral tracer assembly
• Sears extraoral tracer assembly

Intraoral tracers include:
• Microtracer

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The average intercondylar distance which is adequate for complete dentures is:
Explanation:
'A' [Tylman 343]

Intercondylar distance of 110 mm is considered average and adequate for the articulators that exhibit fixed intercondylar distance (Mean value articulators). For example, Mean value articulator (e.g., Hanau H) uses a fixed intercondylar distance of 110 mm.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: The primary cause of Bennett movement is due to contraction of
Explanation:
'B' [Check Explanation Below]

Bennett movement is a lateral jaw movement demarcated by movement of the balancing side condyle. It is brought about by the lateral pterygoid muscle as it is attached to the neck of the condyle on the working side.

Note: The primary cause of Bennett movement (bodily lateral shift of the mandible) is contraction of the medial pterygoid on the working side, causing the condyle to translate laterally.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Posterior palatal seal is present on
Explanation:
'C' [Winkler 2nd ed 110]

Posterior palatal seal is always present on the movable tissues of the soft palate. The PPS must be placed on tissue that can move (soft palate) to create the required seal. The movable nature of the soft palate allows it to adapt to the denture border, creating a seal.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Fovea palatine are
Option A: Structures through which blood supply takes place
Explanation:
'B' [Winkler 2nd ed 109]

Fovea palatinae are mucosal salivary glands (option B). They are indentations near the midline of the palate formed by coalescence of several mucous gland ducts. They are always on the soft palate 2 mm behind the vibrating line. They are found in every individual (option D is also correct but B is the specific answer).

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: During recording of PPS face is tilted down 30 degrees to touch the sternum:
Option A: To activate the muscle of palate & pharynx
Option B: To activate the muscle of soft palate only
Option C: To prevent flow of material to throat
Explanation:
'B' [Winkler 2nd ed 116]

During recording of PPS, the patient's head should be positioned such that the Frankfort horizontal plane is 30 degrees below the horizontal plane (tilted downward touching the sternum). This position ensures the muscles of the soft palate are at their maximum downwards and forward functional position — activating the muscles of the soft palate only (option B). Flexion of the head also prevents aspiration of the impression material and saliva.

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Which of the following is false?
Option A: Posterior palatal seal extends to tuberosity
Option B: Pterygomaxillary seal extends from hamular notch to mucogingival junction
Option C: Pterygomaxillary seal extends using the complete width of hamular notch
Option D: Maxillary denture should be extended to the hamular process
Explanation:
'D' [Refer Synopsis]

The false statement is option D: 'Maxillary denture should be extended to the hamular process.'

The pterygomandibular raphae runs from the pterygoid hamulus and inserts onto the distal end of the mylohyoid ridge. When the mouth is opened wide, the raphae is pulled forward. So the maxillary denture must NOT be extended to the pterygoid hamulus, as it interferes with the raphae. The denture should be extended UP TO the hamular notch (not the hamular process itself).

Subject: Complete Denture
Chapter: Border Moulding and Posterior Palatal Seal
Question: Material of choice for single step border moulding is
Explanation:
'A' [Zarb Bolender 12th ed 226–227]

Material of choice for single step (simultaneous) border moulding is Polyether.

Requirements of material for single step border moulding:
• Have sufficient body to remain in position on borders during loading
• Allow pre-shaping of border form without adhering to fingers
• Setting time of 3–5 minutes
• Retain adequate flow while tray is seated
• Allow finger placement into deficient parts after tray is seated
• Not cause excessive tissue displacement
• Readily trimmed and shaped

Polyether meets all above requirements and can be added in deficient areas while silicone cannot.

Green stick compound is ideally suited for sectional border moulding. It is unsuitable for single step because it is impossible to get the material softened over the full length of the border.

Low viscosity silicone is hydrophobic, lacks sufficient body and does not allow pre-shaping.
